title: The Meme as Replicator
description: Dawkins' analogy and what it means for an idea to be 'alive'

concepts.title: Coining the Term
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Selfish Gene (1976), Richard Dawkins coined meme as the cultural analogue to the gene: a unit of imitation that copies itself from mind to mind.

The Greek root mimēma means 'something imitated'. Dawkins shortened it to rhyme with 'gene'.

Examples he gave: tunes, ideas, catchphrases, fashions, ways of making pots. Anything that propagates by imitation.

concepts.title: Replicator Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
A replicator is anything that makes copies of itself. Genes are replicators built of DNA; memes are replicators built of information.

For Darwinian evolution to operate, you need three ingredients: variation (copies differ), heredity (offspring resemble parents), and differential success (some copy more than others).

Memes have all three. Therefore: ideas evolve.

concepts.title: Memes Don't Need to Help You
concepts.contentHtml:
A meme spreads if it's good at spreading — not if it's good for you. Chain letters are useless to the recipient but excellent at copying.

This is the unsettling core of memetics: ideas can be successful parasites. Doomsday cults, harmful diet fads, conspiracy theories — all can thrive by hijacking attention even while harming hosts.

Think of a meme as a virus made of meaning.

title: Fidelity, Fecundity, Longevity
description: Three properties that make a replicator successful

concepts.title: The Three Properties
concepts.contentHtml:
Dawkins listed three properties that determine how successful a replicator is:

Fidelity — how accurately it copies. High-fidelity copies preserve structure across generations.

Fecundity — how many copies it makes per unit time. A meme spreading person-to-person is slow; one on social media is fast.

Longevity — how long each copy survives. A meme that persists in memory for decades has more chances to spread than one forgotten in an hour.

concepts.title: Mutation by Copy Error
concepts.contentHtml:
Memes mutate when copying fails. Children's playground rhymes drift over generations: 'Ring around the rosie' has dozens of regional variants because each transmission introduces small errors.

Some mutations are neutral (cosmetic word swaps), some lethal (the variant is forgotten), and rare ones are beneficial — they make the meme catchier.

Memetics borrows the term memetic drift: the gradual accumulation of changes through random copy errors.

concepts.title: Why Books Beat Conversations
concepts.contentHtml:
Spoken transmission has low fidelity — every retelling drifts. The Iliad existed for centuries as oral poetry before being written, and it shows in the formulaic phrases poets used as memory anchors.

Writing dramatically increased fidelity. Printing increased fecundity. The internet maxed out both.

The dominant memes of any era are shaped by the medium that carries them.

title: Selection Pressure
description: Why some memes spread and most die forgotten

concepts.title: What Makes a Meme Catchy
concepts.contentHtml:
Memes that spread share recurring traits: emotional intensity (anger, awe, disgust), simplicity (easy to remember and retell), self-reference (the meme tells you to spread it), and identity signaling (sharing it marks you as a member of a tribe).

A study by Berger and Milkman found that high-arousal emotions — both positive (awe) and negative (anger) — predict virality on the New York Times' most-emailed list. Sad articles, despite being moving, spread less.

concepts.title: Memetic Niches
concepts.contentHtml:
Just as species occupy ecological niches, memes compete in cognitive niches: gossip, jokes, recipes, religious doctrine, political slogans.

Within a niche, memes compete for the same attention. Two competing diet fads fight for the same minds; two unrelated memes (a song, a tax theory) don't.

This explains why ecosystems of memes look like ecosystems of organisms — with dominant species, parasites, and the occasional invasive species that wipes out a whole genre.

concepts.title: Truth is Not Required
concepts.contentHtml:
Selection pressure favors spreadability, not truth. Falsehoods spread on Twitter six times faster than verified true statements, according to a 2018 MIT study by Vosoughi et al.

Reasons: false claims are often more novel (novelty drives sharing), more emotionally charged, and unconstrained by reality (so they can be optimized purely for memorability).

Truth has the advantage of being repeatable and durable. Lies have the advantage of being whatever they need to be.

title: Internet Memes & Network Effects
description: Image macros, virality, and platform-shaped evolution

concepts.title: From Dawkins to Doge
concepts.contentHtml:
The popular usage of 'meme' — image macros, reaction GIFs, TikToks — descends from Dawkins via the early-2000s web. O RLY?, lolcats, and Rickrolling were among the first viral templates.

An internet meme is a format with a variable slot. The format is stable (Doge's Comic Sans phrases over a Shiba Inu); the slot is filled with new content (much wow, very replicate).

This separation of chassis and payload is exactly how transposons work in genetics.

concepts.title: Power Laws of Virality
concepts.contentHtml:
Sharing on social networks follows a power law: a tiny fraction of posts get most of the views.

Virality requires not just appeal but structural luck: the right early sharer with a large audience can launch a meme; a better meme posted by a nobody dies. Celebrity-style concentration of followers in a few influencers creates massive variance.

This is why 'going viral' feels random: the underlying distribution has no characteristic scale, and the same post can flop or explode based on early random walks through the network.

concepts.title: Platforms as Selective Environments
concepts.contentHtml:
Each platform applies its own selection pressure. Twitter rewards short, conflict-bait text. TikTok rewards looping audio + dance formats. Reddit rewards inside-joke remix. Instagram once rewarded perfection, now rewards 'authentic' chaos.

Memes evolve to fit their platform like finches evolve to fit their islands. Migration between platforms causes mass extinction events: the LiveJournal meme ecosystem is mostly gone, replaced.

title: Egregores & Memetic Hazards
description: When ideas behave like agents that infect their hosts

concepts.title: The Egregore
concepts.contentHtml:
An egregore (from Greek egrēgoros, 'watcher') is an occult term for a thoughtform — a non-physical entity sustained by collective belief. The concept entered Western occultism via 19th-century French magicians like Eliphas Lévi.

Stripped of mysticism, an egregore is what memetics calls a self-sustaining belief system: a meme complex that recruits new hosts and punishes defection. Brands, fandoms, political tribes, and religions all behave this way.

The egregore 'wants' to persist. It uses its hosts to do so.

concepts.title: Memetic Hazards
concepts.contentHtml:
A memetic hazard is information that damages whoever encounters it — not by physical action but by changing their minds in harmful ways.

Examples: knowledge of a suicide method that increases copycat rates (the Werther effect), information that triggers OCD spirals, doomsday predictions that cause hosts to liquidate assets.

The SCP Foundation popularized the term in fiction, but real-world memetic hazards are documented in epidemiology of suicide and radicalization research. Some libraries deliberately don't catalogue certain manifestos.

concepts.title: Mind Hygiene
concepts.contentHtml:
Memetics suggests an unsettling responsibility: not every idea you hold is yours. Some are passengers that hijacked your attention.

Practical defenses: notice when an idea generates urgency to share it (a copy-fitness signal), trace where you first encountered it, ask who benefits from your belief, and prefer ideas that survive being questioned over ideas that punish doubt.

The strongest defense is meta-awareness: knowing that your mind is a substrate that ideas compete on, you can audit which tenants you let stay.
